textos.27bc8013-cdf5-4ce5-b3c5-7d7ef5a09e31#291: To determine the fields in a table, decide what you need to know about the people, things, or events recorded in the table. You can think of fields as attributes of the table. Each record (or row) in the table contains the same set of fields or attributes. For example, an address field in a customer table contains customers' addresses. Each record in the table contains data about one customer, and the address field contains the address for that customer.

**Identifying Fields**
Provides tips for determining the fields you might need in your database.
**Using Primary Key Fields**
Explains how each table in your database should include a field or set of fields that uniquely identifies each individual record stored in the table, for [[T0]] to work most efficiently.

**Designing Databases**
Take advantage of relational database technology in [[T0]] with well-planned databases.
**Working with Tables**
Describes how to make sure your tables have the structure that your application requires. Data type and index choices are essential to the success of your application.
**Working with Fields**

Enables or disables modal states for distributable [[T0]] .exe automation servers.

[[C0]]

**0**
Enables unattended mode. When unattended mode is enabled, a [[T0]] error is generated whenever a modal state occurs. Your .exe automation server can trap for these errors with an [[T1]] routine.
**1**
(Default) Disables unattended mode. Modal states, which require user intervention, can occur. Unattended mode is disabled at startup.

Use [[T0]](2335) to enable or disable modal states in [[T1]] .exe automation servers. Automation servers are created with the Project Manager. For additional information about using [[T2]] to create .exe automation servers, see Sharing Information and Adding [[T3]].

Modal states occur when dialogs or errors messages are displayed, requiring input from a user to exit the dialog or error message and continue program execution. Modal states can be undesirable in .exe servers that are deployed remotely, possibly without intervention from a user. Program execution is halted, and requires intervention for program execution to continue.

The following table lists some typical examples of modal states that can occur in an .exe server.

| Modal State | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| [[T4]] command or [[T5]] function | Can occur in program code. |
| [[T6]] errors such as "File access is denied" or "Allowed [[T7]] nesting level exceeded" | Can occur in program code. |
| Open dialog boxes | Can occur when files included in a [[T8]] statement cannot be located. |
| [[T9]] Connection Login dialog box | Can occur after a connection cannot be established. |

[[T10]](2335 ,0) should be executed as soon as possible in unattended .exe automation server program code because a modal state can occur anytime after program execution begins.

Note that [[T0]](2335) applies only to .exe automation servers for which the StartMode property equals 2 or 4. Unattended mode is always enabled for in-process .dll automation servers (for which the StartMode property equals 3).

Issuing [[T1]](2335) without an argument in a runtime application returns its current setting.

Returns or sets current column number.

[[C0]]

_PCOLNO is included for backward compatibility. Use the Report Writer instead.

_PCOLNO contains a numeric value that establishes the current column position. You can use _PCOLNO to determine the next column address for output. As [[T0]] sends output to the print device, it automatically increments the _PCOLNO value to indicate the current column position.

You can assign any integer value to _PCOLNO, from 0 to 255, in order to position output to a desired column. Assigning a value to _PCOLNO has the same effect as using the [[T1]] clause of the ? command.

This dialog box makes it possible for you to search for and replace specified text in the current file. To replace within tables, click Replace Field on the Table menu. The keyboard shortcut to access this dialog box is [[T0]]+L.
 **Look For**
Specifies the text string to search for.
**Replace With**
Specifies the replacement text.
**Options**
Defines the limits and direction of the search and replace. If you specify text to search for and do not get the expected results, make sure you have the following options selected: Match Case Replaces text that exactly matches the combination of uppercase and lowercase letters you type in the Look For box. Wrap Around Searches the current file, from the insertion point to the end of the file, and then from the beginning of the file to the original insertion point. Match Whole Word Replaces distinct occurrences of words, except for embedded text. Search Backward Searches backwards from the current insertion point to the beginning of the file. Use wildcards Makes it possible for you to use wildcard characters in your search text.
**Scope**
Defines how extensive the search is. The Scope options are enabled when you are editing a procedure in a Code window. Current Procedure Searches only the current procedure, which is displayed in the Code window. Current Object Searches all procedures (event code) in the current (selected) object. All Objects Searches all procedures (event code) in all objects in the current form or form set.
**Find Next**
Finds the next occurrence of the string you typed in the Look For box. This button is not enabled until you type text in the Look For box.
**Replace**
Changes the selected text to the text in the Replace With box. If you want to leave the selected text unchanged and move to the next occurrence, click Find Next .
**Replace All**
Finds and replaces all instances of the text in the Find What box with the text in the Replace With box. You can undo the replacements by choosing the Undo command.

textos.291ca481-a1bf-4a78-ac59-da3dfaba4037#302: [[T0]](1037) displays the Page Setup dialog box so you can change printer settings such as the paper size and orientation. The settings available in the Page Setup dialog box depend on the printer installed. [[T1]](1037) also sets the printer environment settings for the report to the default printer settings or the default printer settings to the report printer environment settings. For more information, see Page Setup Dialog Box ([[T2]]).

[[T0]](1037,1), [[T1]](1037,2), and [[T2]](1037,3) are primarily useful for developers working with [[T3]] 9.0 Report System extension features. For more information about these features, see Extending Report Functionality in [[T4]].

All three report-related [[T5]](1037,<N>) variants require access to a cursor or open table with the same format as a report (.frx) or label (.lbx) definition file. The report must be selected as a cursor or opened as a table before you call the function, and [[T6]] requires the report table to be opened exclusively. Otherwise, an error occurs when you call the function. For more information about the structure of report and label tables, see Table Structures of Table Files (.dbc, .frx, .lbx, .mnx, .pjx, .scx, .vcx).

[[T7]](1037,1) provides a way for developers implementing Report Builder extensions to invoke the native page setup dialog box and persist the user's choices directly to a report or label table. For more information, see Extending Reports at Design Time.

[[T0]](1037,2) serves as a way to save current printer settings to a cursor temporarily so you can restore the printer environment later. As such, this function always stores complete details to the cursor you provide. If this cursor is a real report, and did not have a printer environment saved to it before you used [[T1]](1037,2), it has a complete printer environment saved to it afterwards. If you do not want printer environment details to remain in this cursor, it is your responsibility to clear out the relevant fields later. To avoid the need to perform this cleanup task, simply provide a temporary cursor in the correct format with one record in it, rather than using a real report or label with [[T2]](1037,2). For more information, see How to: Save the Printer Environment for Reports.

[[T3]](1037,2) preserves any information already in the report's printer environment settings. It adds settings that are not currently in the report's printer environment, and does not overwrite existing settings.

For example, if a report definition includes [[I0]] and [[I1]], to specify a landscape report and three printed copies, the default printer environment will not overwrite this setting with a portrait orientation. However, if you remove the line specifying [[I2]] from the report definition before calling the function, the report definition will include a [[I3]] line after calling the function. This line will match the current [[T0]] default.

Because this behavior is additive, if you want to save the full default [[T1]] default printer environment, you should use an empty cursor with this function, or make sure the relevant fields are completely empty before calling [[T2]](1037,2).

[[T0]](1037,3) restores printer settings from a report definition to the current [[T1]] default. Although it may seem counter-intuitive, using this variant of the function requires complete printer environment information in the report or label, and therefore may write data to the cursor as well as changing the default printer environment. If your report or label did not have complete information before you used the function, it will have complete information after you use it.

In previous versions of [[T0]], saving printer settings in reports used three fields in the table's first record: the [[T1]], [[T2]], and [[T3]] fields. In [[T4]] 9.0, if you choose not to save Printer Environment with a report, much less information is stored in these fields, making it possible for your report to work more appropriately with a wider variety of printers.

In [[T5]] 9.0, when you design reports, you can also override any settings stored in these fields by using a fourth field, [[T6]], in first record. Your stored settings in [[T7]] override any settings for the same printer attributes in the [[T8]] and [[T9]] fields. Note that these settings are case-sensitive.

[[T10]](1037) is aware of user settings in [[T11]] and takes them into account when restoring printer environment from a report or label file.

When you run reports or labels, users may have yet another level of override of stored printer settings: the [[T12]] clause on [[T13]] and [[T14]] commands. If you use this keyword, or if you provide equivalent instructions with a ReportListener object's [[T15]] member, any settings provided by the user at runtime take precedence over settings stored in the report as well as default [[T16]] printer environment settings. For more information, see [[T17]] Command, [[T18]] Command, and CommandClauses Property.

Commands and functions can accept expressions as parameters, or they can appear in expressions. You can also use user-defined functions (UDFs) whenever you can use a [[T1]] command or function.

Commands and functions behave differently:
 - Commands perform an action. For example, you can use the [[T2]] command to look at the contents of a table.
- Functions return a value of a given data type. For example, the [[T3]] function returns the system date from your computer. Functions end with a pair of parentheses that distinguish them from commands.

Functions are not used by themselves, but are always combined with a [[T4]] command. For example, the question mark (?) is a command that sends output to the screen. [[T5]] is a function that returns the current system date. You can combine them to output the system date to the screen:
